junction.name: Hamilton Avenue & Court Street, New York City

claims.text: Hamilton Avenue & Court Street had 79 injury crashes in police records since 2021-10-31: 5 pedestrians injured, 2 cyclists injured and 0 people killed.
At the U.S. DOT's values that harm costs about $5.4 million a year.
39% of crashes here had only people in vehicles hurt, against 24% at the city's priority junctions.
15% of crashes here had “following too closely” recorded as a contributing factor, against 6% at the city's priority junctions.
7% of crashes here had “unsafe lane changing” recorded as a contributing factor, against 2% at the city's priority junctions.

Held up on later years: a vehicle was hit on the center back end in 42% of crashes since 2024-05-01, against 18% at the city's priority junctions (found by the greedy search and the exhaustive search).

Held up on later years: a vehicle was going straight ahead, heading west and no one hurt in 33% of crashes since 2024-05-01, against 10% at the city's priority junctions (found by the exhaustive search).

The city's Leading Pedestrian Interval signals: passed the causal gate (pedestrian injury crashes changed -17% (95% interval -22% to -11%) at 1,651 sites against sites treated later or the citywide trend, and a placebo date shows nothing).
The city's turn traffic calming: earlier trend (a simple before/after says -26%, but a placebo date before the work shows a drop too, so the decline cannot be credited to the program).
The city's enhanced crossings: not shown (at 96 sites the change in pedestrian injury crashes (-7%, 95% interval -50% to +69%) could be zero).
The city's speed humps: not shown (at 1,008 sites the change in injury crashes (+0%, 95% interval -9% to +9%) could be zero).

Backplates with Retroreflective Borders would avoid about 2.4 crashes a year (CMF 1410, the record FHWA's fact sheet cites; evidence: only if a site check confirms it), worth $811,000 a year; check on site: an entry on yellow or red.

Yellow Change Intervals would avoid about 1.2 crashes a year (CMF 4219, the more conservative of the two middle records of 4; evidence: only if a site check confirms it), worth $422,000 a year; check on site: an entry on yellow or red; the current yellow plus all-red time is below the ITE recommended practice.
The New York State Department of Transportation (NYSDOT), Region 11 is responsible for BKLYN/QUEENS EXP (I 278), Gowanus Expressway (I 278) (owner recorded in NYSDOT Roadway Inventory).
The NYC Department of Transportation (NYC DOT) is responsible for Hamilton Avenue, Court Street (not listed in NYSDOT Roadway Inventory, so a city street).
Who can push for it: Council Member, District 38, New York City Council; Brooklyn Community Board 6.
A request letter to the New York State Department of Transportation (NYSDOT), Region 11 and the NYC Department of Transportation (NYC DOT) is drafted and checked.

draft_request.letter:
To: the New York State Department of Transportation (NYSDOT), Region 11; the NYC Department of Transportation (NYC DOT)
Cc: Council Member, District 38, New York City Council; Brooklyn Community Board 6
Subject: Request for safety review at Hamilton Avenue & Court Street

Dear colleagues at NYSDOT Region 11 and NYC DOT,

We write to ask each agency to carry out a safety study at Hamilton Avenue & Court Street for the roads it is responsible for and to make the fixes where they are warranted.

The official record for the 5 years from 31 October 2021 shows 186 crashes, with 79 injury crashes. Five pedestrians and 2 cyclists were injured. No one was killed. The NYC Department of Transportation marks this as a priority location. The yearly harm is about $5.4 million when costed in the U.S. DOT's official values for the cost of crashes (2024 dollars). The latest recorded safety project is Hamilton Ave and Court St in 2025.

On your roads, please consider:

* longer yellow signal times, which is expected to prevent about 4.3 injury crashes a year and avoid about $1,471,000 of harm a year, after a site check for an entry on yellow or red. This would pay for itself if it costs under $10.3 million.
* reflective backplates on the traffic signals, which is expected to prevent about 2.4 injury crashes a year and avoid about $811,000 of harm a year, after a site check for an entry on yellow or red. This would pay for itself if it costs under $5.7 million.

In New York City, a leading pedestrian interval (a walk signal a few seconds before the green) was also studied: where the city installed it at 1,651 intersections, pedestrian injury crashes fell 17% (95% interval 11% to 22%) compared with intersections that got it later; a stricter check against fake programs is less certain, and needs a site check for a turning movement.

Thank you for your attention.

[Your name]
[Your organisation or address]

Sources:
- NYC Open Data, Motor Vehicle Collisions - Crashes (h9gi-nx95)
- NYC DOT Street Improvement Projects (corridors); NYC DOT Street Improvement Projects (intersections); NYC Vision Zero View, Enhanced Crossings (6ax4-q5k4); NYC Vision Zero View, Leading Pedestrian Interval Signals; NYC Vision Zero View, Signal Timing/25 MPH Retiming; NYC Vision Zero View, Speed Humps (jknp-skuy); NYC Vision Zero View, Turn Traffic Calming; NYC Vision Zero priority corridors; NYC Vision Zero priority intersections
- FHWA CMF Clearinghouse, CMF 4215 (longer yellow signal times)
- FHWA CMF Clearinghouse, CMF 1410 (reflective backplates on the traffic signals)
- U.S. DOT Benefit-Cost Analysis Guidance, 2026 Update, Table A-1 (2024 dollars)
- NearMissLens NML-Bench T11: before/after study of the city's own installs (validation/BENCH.md)
- Road owners: the registry's road-inventory layer (see the engineer report's receipts)
